Strengths of this work: SceneForge is a general framework that can be easily integrated with other 3D encoders. It can improve performance on a wide range of tasks and benchmarks. The method is simple yet effective, supported by comprehensive experiments.

The rebuttal effectively addressed reviewers' major concerns and clearly explained the technical contributions of the work. As a result, the final decision is to accept the paper.

As the discussion period comes to a close, we would like to express our sincere gratitude for your reviews and discussions. We were encouraged that reviewers found our method to be effective, general and model-agnostic, with comprehensive experiments showing clear and consistent improvements on multiple downstream tasks.

We are especially grateful that this process has directly led to substantial additions that we believe significantly strengthen our paper's impact and analysis. Thanks to your insightful suggestions, we conducted and analyzed new experiments which we will integrate into the final manuscript and supplementary material. These new contributions include:

- A preliminary analysis of the point cloud sampling budget, showing how performance is affected by scene complexity and providing guidance for future work.

- A quantitative analysis focusing on the ScanQA benchmark, demonstrating our method's strong generalization to more complex, unseen spatial relations not used during pre-training.

- A comprehensive new evaluation of supervised fine-tuning on multiple classification benchmarks. These results show that our pre-training consistently boosts performance for both full fine-tuning and, crucially, several state-of-the-art Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods on both synthetic and challenging real-world data.

We are very pleased that the rebuttals and discussions have allowed us to thoroughly address the questions and concerns raised during the review process.

Although the discussion period is ending soon, we are still available to answer any final questions you may have.

Thank you again for your engagement. We are confident that these new results and clarifications have strengthened our work, and we hope to have earned your support.

Sincerely,

The Authors

We sincerely thank you for your valuable feedback and appreciate your patience while we conducted the suggested evaluations. 

We agree that analyzing more supervised fine-tuning tasks is a crucial addition. We were indeed very interested in this direction and had already conducted full fine-tuning in our post-submission experiments, which we include to serve as a reference baseline. However, your suggestion to employ Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning methods was particularly insightful, especially for mitigating potential overfitting on large-scale models like Uni3D, which is the best but biggest transformer backbone in our work.

Following your recommendation, we have conducted new experiments using multiple PEFT approaches: a traditional Adapter [1], DAPT [2], and PointGST [3]. We performed these evaluations on three key classification benchmarks: the synthetic ModelNet40, the more challenging, real-world ScanObjectNN (OBJ_ONLY as in the paper) and ScanNet object instances directly extracted from scenes through semantic masks (following the ScanNet evaluation of previous models such as Uni3D and $CLIP^2$), thus addressing also indoor scene data as requested.

We based on official implementations and standard hyperparameters to ensure a fair comparison. Specifically, for the traditional Adapter, we used a bottleneck dimension of m=32 to maintain a comparable parameter count to other methods. For DAPT, we used the recommended adapter dimension of r=64. For PointGST, we used the standard adapter dimension of r=36, s=1 and k=4 local groups.

Below, we present the table with the results obtained:

|Model|Method|Trainable Params|ModelNet40|ScanObjectNN| ScanNet Instances |
|:---|:---|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
|Uni3D | full fine tuning | 1016.5M (100%) | 94.28 | 97.12 | 82.72 |
|SF-Uni3D | full fine tuning | 1016.5M (100%) | 94.42 | 97.58 | 83.58 |
|||||||
|Uni3D | Adapter | 7.6M (0.74%) | 94.35 | 96.80 | 81.42 |
|SF-Uni3D | Adapter | 7.6M (0.74%) | 94.46 | 97.09 | 82.56 |
|| | | | | |
| Uni3D | DAPT | 7.3M (0.72%) | 94.33 | 96.78 | 82.65 |
| SF-Uni3D | DAPT | 7.3M (0.72%) | 94.49 | 97.15 | 83.46 |
| | | | | | |
| Uni3D | PointGST | 4.11M (0.4%) | 94.83 | 97.68 | 83.04 |
| SF-Uni3D | PointGST | 4.11M (0.4%) | 94.95 | 98.09 | 84.29 |

We extract three main observations:

1. SCENEFORGE provides a stronger and more generalizable initialization.
As clearly shown by the results, our compositional pre-training with SCENEFORGE provides a significantly more robust initialization for downstream tasks. For every fine-tuning method used, the SF-Uni3D backbone consistently outperforms the baseline Uni3D. This confirms that the richer, more diverse representations learned during pre-training are not limited to improving zero-shot capabilities but provide a solid foundation that translates into superior performance even in supervised fine-tuning scenarios. This observation is consistent with the findings already present in our paper for 3D VQA and part segmentation, where a better pretrained model led to better fine-tuned results.

2. The benefit of SCENEFORGE scales with task complexity.
The impact of our method is modulated by the complexity of the dataset. On ModelNet40, a dataset of synthetic and "clean" objects, the performance is already near saturation, so the gain provided by SCENEFORGE is limited but still present. On ScanObjectNN, which introduces real-world noise and occlusions, the advantage of SF-Uni3D becomes more apparent. Crucially, on ScanNet Instances, involving objects extracted from complex indoor scenes, the benefit of SF-Uni3D is most pronounced. This further supports the idea that our framework is most valuable for learning robust features that can be transferred to complex real-world data.

3. Results highlight a powerful synergy between SCENEFORGE-pretraining and state-of-the-art 3D PEFT strategies. Indeed,  our pretraining allows not only full fine tuning, but also PEFT methods to reach higher performance peaks. Notably, fine tuning with PointGST obtains the best results, not only outperforming other PEFT methods but even surpassing full fine-tuning across all datasets, while using a mere 0.4% of the trainable parameters. This result validates our pretraining effectiveness and the reviewer's hint that fully fine-tuning these large models can be suboptimal, likely due to overfitting, showing that PEFT methods can be a more effective strategy for downstream tasks.

We hope these experiments addressed your comments and substantially elevated the paper's contribution. We will integrate this analysis and the results into the next version.

Thank you once again for your constructive participation. We hope these positive results earn your full support.

[1] Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning for NLP, ICML 19 [2] Dynamic Adapter Meets Prompt Tuning: Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning for Point Cloud Analysis. CVPR 24 [3] Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning in Spectral Domain for Point Cloud Learning. TPAMI 25

Thank you. Based on the current content of the paper, most of my questions have been addressed. However, I believe that the current focus is on some simple tasks, primarily zero-shot tasks. I suggest exploring whether the framework's text alignment improves supervised fine-tuning performance on tasks beyond zero-shot, such as classification, potentially including indoor scene tasks. While larger models may overfit, parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods [1-2] (or a discussion of PointBERT) could be beneficial.

Incorporating these points could improve the article's visibility. I am willing to raise my score if positive results are observed. If supplementary experiments are not feasible within the rebuttal period, I will still keep a positive score and recommend including the suggested discussions in the final version.

[2] Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning in Spectral Domain for Point Cloud Learning. TPAMI 25

We thank the reviewer for their insightful feedback and constructive suggestions. We are encouraged that the reviewer found our method to be general, our experimental results comprehensive, and the improvements clear. We will address the weaknesses and questions raised point-by-point.

### W1: Latency and Resource Overhead
We provide a detailed analysis of latency and resource overhead in the supplementary material (Sec. 5), for which we briefly report the results in the main document (Sec. 3.2). We will reference the supplementary analysis more prominently in the main paper upon acceptance. To summarize the key findings for the reviewer's convenience:

First, our method introduces no practical deployment latency: at inference time, the computational cost is identical to the baseline model, as the model architecture and forward pass are unchanged.

The additional computational overhead from our method is confined entirely to the training stage as a one-time, offline cost. The point cloud combination cost is negligible, as it is composed just by fast operations as uniform sampling of samples and positional relations, and then 3D transformations and array concatenations. Instead, the LLM-based caption refinement does introduce an overhead, which however we show can be effectively eliminated (Supplementary Sec. 5). For instance, by using quantized LLM replicas on a single GPU, the training overhead is removed even for the fastest backbones. Therefore, our method delivers significant performance gains without compromising the efficiency required for practical deployment. 

### W2: Benefits for part segmentation and classification
We thank the reviewer for highlighting this aspect, as it allows us to further clarify the mechanisms behind the performance improvements. We will address the benefits for part segmentation and single-object classification separately.

- On the Benefit for Part Segmentation. 

    Our hypothesis is that compositional training encourages the model to learn more fine-grained, part-aware features, which serve as a superior starting point for the few-shot part segmentation task. To correctly interpret composite scenes which change at every sampling (both in subjects and relation), the model is discouraged from simply learning a holistic representation. It it pushed instead to first learn to distinguish the constituent objects ("hat," "person") before it can reason about their spatial relationship ("over"). This process implicitly forces the 3D encoder to develop more localized and semantically meaningful features that can isolate object parts. Because the downstream part-segmentation task is performed in a few-shot setting, the quality of the pretrained encoder is critical. By pretraining on our compositional scenes, the encoder is already primed to understand part-level relationships, providing a much stronger feature representation for the lightweight segmentation heads to fine-tune from. The consistent gains shown in Table 2 of our main paper support this conclusion.

- On the Benefit for Single-Object Classification. 

    Our approach is directly inspired by a well-established principle from representation learning literature: multi-sample augmentations act as powerful regularizers. In 2D vision, techniques like MixUp and CutMix are proven to enhance model robustness and generalization. They do so by creating diverse, challenging training samples that encourage the learning of smoother decision boundaries. Just as MixUp and CutMix pair their augmented images with corresponding soft labels, our method pairs its composite 3D scenes with rich, LLM-refined textual scene descriptions. This descriptive caption effectively functions as a semantic soft label. Instead of merely interpolating class probabilities, it weaves together multiple distinct concepts and their spatial relations into a single, refined target description. This parallel is particularly potent in our zero-shot context, where text prompts are the labels at inference time. By training the encoder to align with these complex "semantic soft labels," we directly encourage a more organized and discriminative feature space. Ultimately, this structured composition of both the 3D input and the textual "label" forces the model to understand each object's features within a complex relational context, yielding a more robust representation that generalizes effectively to the simpler task of single-object classification.

    To provide direct quantitative evidence for this, we did analyze the cosine margin, a standard metric for evaluating the quality of a learned representation space. The margin is defined as the difference between the cosine similarity of a sample to its correct (positive) class and the similarity to its most confusing incorrect (hardest negative) class. A larger margin indicates better class separation and a more robust model.

    The results below show that our SCENEFORGE (SF) method consistently and significantly improves this margin across all three backbones and all four benchmark datasets.

    Crucially, on the most challenging datasets (LVIS and ScanNet), where baselines often exhibit a negative margin, meaning they are more confident in an incorrect class than the correct one, our method provides the largest improvements. For example, SF-Uni3D pushes the LVIS margin from negative to positive.     We thank the reviewer for the insightful question: upon acceptance, we will add these results, as it was our intention, to the supplementary material. We will also improve the explaination of the mechanisms behind the benefits in the already dedicated main document section.

## Questions
- ScanNet: as mentioned in the paper, we follow previous works (Uni3D, CLIP^2) for the Scannet Evaluation. Instance classification is performed on extracted object instances, not entire scenes. Objects are extracted with the instance masks provided by the dataset, and the ones with fewer than 5 points are removed. The task is zero-shot recognition on the common 17-class split (VoteNet, H3dnet). Classification logits are computed by comparing an instance's 3D features to text prompt features (e.g., "point cloud of {CLASS}").
- ScanObjNN: As per Scannet, we adopt the benchmark from Uni3D for direct comparison, using the OBJ_ONLY variant without colors.

We trust that our detailed overhead analysis, new quantitative evidence on representation quality via cosine margins, and clarifications on our experimental protocols directly address the reviewer's initial concerns and questions. We believe these additions substantially strengthen our contribution and we would be grateful if the reviewer would consider them in their final assessment of the paper. We thank the reviewer for their detailed analysis and for recognizing our "exceptionally thorough and rigorous experiments." We appreciate the opportunity to clarify why SCENEFORGE is a methodological contribution, not an incremental augmentation.

We agree that our work is data-centric, and we argue this is precisely where its methodological novelty lies. In a field where architectural improvements can yield diminishing returns, we demonstrate that innovating on the learning signal itself is a powerful and novel frontier. Here's why:

- Data-Centric Novelty: The novelty of SCENEFORGE lies in its structured manipulation of the input-label space, a powerful way to regularize the model and improve its representations. This approach of innovating on the learning signal itself, rather than the architecture, is precisely why foundational 2D methods like MixUp and CutMix were considered novel. SCENEFORGE introduces a similar principle to the 3D-text domain, but goes further by composing scenes that preserve object semantics while injecting new, structured relational information.

- Fundamentally Alters the Learning Task: We shift the objective from only object recognition to a more complex task including contextual scene understanding. By introducing in the batch structured 3D scenes with LLM-refined scene captions, we force the model to learn spatial relationships and part-whole reasoning. Our experiments prove this is crucial for enhancing the model's spatial reasoning and generalization.

- Structured Composition, Not Direct Mixing: Unlike direct augmentations like PointMixup, our structured forging process ensures geometric and semantic coherence. Our ablation study (Table 4) proves this structured approach is the key to our performance.

- Novelty Validated by Impact: Our framework's impact is the strongest evidence of its novelty. The fact that our single model outperforms a powerful SOTA ensemble (OmniBind) shows that a better learning signal can be more impactful than adding architectural complexity.

We hope this clarifies our perspective. We believe this reframes SCENEFORGE as a novel methodological contribution, and we will gladly revise the manuscript to emphasize these points more clearly.

## Questions
Q1: LLM ablation

We agree that ablating the LLM component in the pipeline is crucial. We ran this exact experiment (Supp. Table 2): we compare our full method (using Qwen 2.5) against a variant that uses raw, template-based captions without any LLM refinement (SF-Uni3D/NO LLM). These raw captions are constructed by simply concatenating object descriptions with spatial relations (e.g., "[object1] next to [object2]"), which is analogous to the reviewer's proposed template-based approach. The "NO LLM" variant, which uses only structured 3D scenes and template-based text, already shows clear improvements over the Uni3D baseline across all benchmarks. However, refining these raw captions with an LLM provides a second, significant boost in performance. We also report and observe similar boost also with LLama 3.1 instead of Qwen 2.5.

Q2: Failure cases. 

On the point-cloud composition side, our choices of positional relationship and the method we propose to apply them ensures us that no failure cases can occurr. For the LLM side, there are possible cases of hallucination and information alteration. To analyze LLM failure cases, following the reviewer insightful question, we built an automated verification pipeline using dependency parsing with spaCy (classic NLP). This tool programmatically extracts subjects (nouns) and their descriptive attributes (adjectives), and we do that for both the raw concatenated captions and the final refined captions. We ran this check on 1M random combined scene captions with SCENEFORGE, and we found that in over 98% of cases, original subjects and their attributes were perfectly preserved. In the ~2% failure cases, 79% of them are for wrong attributes (attribute binding is indeed a very well known problem of LLMs), 20% are missing attributes and just 1% is about wrong subjects. Even with this unfrequent possible failure cases, the use of the LLM for rewriting brings crucial benefits to the pipeline, as discussed in the previous point.

Q3: d vector

d in the xy-plane is re-sampled randomly for each "next to" placement, and it is identified by uniform sampling its angle wrt x axis. Inside single scenes, we only check for intersections with previous placed objects in case of #objects > 2 to avoid unrealistic scenes, and in that case we resample it. This allows us to produce all valid and variegate positionings in the considered potential scene.

rebuttal.value:
We are deeply grateful to the reviewer for their positive and encouraging feedback, their high rating of our work, and their insightful questions. We are glad they found our method's impact to be large, model-agnostic, and our analysis thorough. We will address the points raised below.

We agree with the reviewer that our current placement strategy is a simplified abstraction of real-world interactions and does not explicitly model fine-grained geometry like placing an object on a shelf. This was a deliberate design choice aimed at creating a robust, scalable, and general-purpose augmentation method. Implementing more complex relations like "laying on top of" or "inside" would require detailed, object-specific knowledge. For example, "laying on" would necessitate identifying suitable planar surfaces on the target object, while "inside" would require semantic knowledge about which objects can be containers.

Enforcing such constraints would have severely limited our compositions or training data itself to smaller, highly-curated datasets where this information is available. This would forfeit the primary advantage of leveraging massive, diverse, and less-curated datasets like Objaverse, which is critical for learning generalizable representations.

Therefore, we opted for a small set of universal and object-agnostic spatial relations. These simple relations can be applied to any pair of objects without prior knowledge, ensuring maximum scalability. Despite their simplicity, they are foundational for spatial understanding and, as our results demonstrate, provide a powerful training signal. Our strong performance on the ScanQA VQA benchmark and the object repositioning task  confirm that the model effectively learns meaningful spatial reasoning from these cues. We see this as a foundational step. As mentioned in our Limitations section (Sec. 6), incorporating more sophisticated, semantically-aware priors is a promising future direction that can build upon the strong, general-purpose base established by our current approach.


We thank again the reviewer: in the camera ready version, we will make more clear the just explained motivations behind our dseign choices for the considered positional relations.
## Questions
- How are relations + objects sampled? As highlighted above, thanks to the universal applicability of our relations, we can sample both the additional objects and the spatial relations uniformly at random from the training set and our predefined relation set, respectively. In each scene, objects are sampled without replacement to avoid ambiguities, while relations are sampled with replacement to allow a greater variability.


- About plausibility: the reviewer rightly notes that this random sampling can lead to semantically implausible scenes. We believe indeed that even implausible scenes can be helpful. By exposing the model to a vast and diverse set of combinations, both plausible and implausible, we push it to learn disentangled and robust features for individual objects. To understand an unlikely scene, the model must first develop a strong, independent understanding of each component. This process is analogous to aspects of human learning. We can easily imagine fantastical or absurd scenes, and this ability to compose known concepts in novel ways strengthens, rather than weakens, our understanding of the concepts themselves. Moreover, filtering unplausible scenes would require additional knowledge or limiting the available data, which falls into the same data quality-scale tradeoff described above.

    Furthermore, it is crucial to distinguish between the types of "implausibility" our method generates versus the ones we discussed above with complex relations:

    - Our method creates scenes that may be semantically implausible but remain geometrically coherent. For example, a "a planet next to a dinosaur" is unlikely but physically possible to arrange. The spatial relationship is simple and universally applicable.

    - We instead avoid creating scenes that are geometrically nonsensical, such as " a planet inside a dinosaur." This would require complex, object-specific modifications (like cutting a hole) that would break the geometric integrity, and possibly semantic properties, of the shapes and create a confusing learning signal to align with the caption.

- Did we notice problems with implausible scenes? Our experiments indicate that our training strategy is beneficial: when the encoder is used as a feature extractor for downstream tasks requiring strong semantic reasoning, such as ScanQA evaluation, our method consistently outperforms the baseline. We did perform a qualitative review of failure cases in the VQA task, but we did not find any significant pattern suggesting that training on implausible scenes led to specific types of errors in real data.

- For Image renderings, we stick with the approach from the baseline model Uni3D for fairness, rendering 10 color images from different views that uniformly cover the whole shape, then we uniformly sample one of 10 each time during training steps.

Thank you once again for your valuable feedback and strong support. We hope these clarifications have fully addressed your questions.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
1. The ideas are simple but effective. This method delivers consistent gains across multiple 3D-text alignment benchmarks.

1. The set of predefined spatial relations is too limited, so it fails to capture more complex or subtle spatial arrangements.
2. Using a fixed 10k point sampling budget causes performance to drop sharply when four or more objects appear. It would help to see results with more points such as 10k, 20k, and 40k points to understand how sampling affects accuracy.

questions.value:
1. Is it possible to include more spatial relationships and construct a more complex scene for training?
2. Refer to point 2 of Weaknesses.

summary.value: This paper introduces SCENEFORGE, a novel data augmentation framework designed to enhance contrastive learning alignment between 3D point clouds and text by constructing structured, multi-object 3D scenes. The core idea is to utilize individual 3D object point clouds and combine them into complex scenes based on predefined, explicit spatial relations (e.g., "over," "under," "next to"). Simultaneously, the method leverages a Large Language Model (LLM), specifically Qwen2.5, to "forge" the individual object text descriptions into a single, coherent, and natural scene description that accurately reflects the spatial layout. By mixing these synthetic "compositional" samples with original single-object samples in training batches, SCENEFORGE effectively increases the diversity and complexity of the training data, thereby alleviating the scarcity of large-scale 3D-text datasets.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
1. While most contemporary work focuses on improving model architectures, SCENEFORGE takes a unique, data-centric approach, proposing a model-agnostic, plug-and-play framework. Through the "scene forging" process, it not only virtually expands the dataset but, more importantly, introduces "harder samples" with structured and relational information, which is crucial for enhancing a model's generalization and spatial reasoning capabilities.
2. The authors have conducted exceptionally thorough and rigorous experiments to validate their method's efficacy.
3. Not only does SCENEFORGE achieve consistent gains over all baselines, but its SF-Uni3D variant also outperforms the powerful ensemble model OmniBind on several zero-shot classification benchmarks. 

Weaknesses:
While the results presented in this paper are strong, I have significant reservations about the novelty of the core methodology. At its heart, the proposed method, SCENEFORGE, is a direct data augmentation technique. It does not introduce a new model architecture or a fundamental change to the contrastive learning framework itself.
The contribution is primarily at the data level—synthesizing more complex and diverse training samples by composing existing ones. Although this is executed cleverly with the use of an LLM for caption refinement, the overall approach can be framed as an advanced form of data engineering rather than a novel method in representation learning. The work, despite its effectiveness, may be perceived as incremental from a methodological standpoint.

questions.value:
1. The success of SCENEFORGE appears to stem from a combination of factors: stronger spatial relationship modeling, more challenging contrastive samples, and richer linguistic descriptions from the LLM. Could you design an experiment to try and disentangle the contributions of these factors? For example, what would the performance be if you used a fixed template (e.g., "A model of [object1] is [relation] a model of [object2]") to generate captions, without refinement from the LLM? This would help isolate the precise contribution of the LLM "forging" process.

2. To better understand the method's boundaries, could you provide an analysis of some failure cases? For instance, are there certain object combinations or spatial relationships that SCENEFORGE struggles to generate or align correctly? Or, in what situations does the LLM produce erroneous or ambiguous scene descriptions?

3. In the methods section, you mention that the "next to" placement is achieved by sampling a horizontal unit vector d. How is this vector d sampled? Is it re-sampled randomly for each placement, or is it consistent for all "next to" relationships within a single composed scene? This detail could affect the naturalness of the scene layouts.

4. As noted in the paper, the fixed point budget and simple spatial relations are current limitations. What do you believe is the best path forward to address this? Is it simply a matter of increasing the point budget (e.g., having it scale dynamically with the number of objects N), or are more intelligent point cloud sampling strategies needed to preserve salient geometric features? On the spatial relations front, how could a richer set of relations be introduced in a cost-effective manner?

5. The experiments show that α=0.5 is an optimal choice. This value seems intuitive (half single samples, half composed samples). Do you believe this optimal value is universal? Might it change depending on the capacity of the backbone model, the characteristics of the dataset, or the number of combined objects N?

title.value: SceneForge: Enhancing 3D-text alignment with Structured Scene Compositions

abstract.value: The whole is greater than the sum of its parts, even in 3D-text contrastive learning. We introduce SceneForge, a novel framework that enhances contrastive alignment between 3D point clouds and text through structured multi-object scene compositions. SceneForge leverages individual 3D shapes to construct multi-object scenes with explicit spatial relations, pairing them with coherent multi-object descriptions refined by a large language model. By augmenting contrastive training with these structured, compositional samples, SceneForge effectively addresses the scarcity of large-scale 3D-text datasets, significantly enriching data complexity and diversity. We systematically investigate critical design elements, such as the optimal number of objects per scene, the proportion of compositional samples in training batches, and scene construction strategies. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SceneForge delivers substantial performance gains across multiple tasks, including zero-shot classification on ModelNet, ScanObjNN, Objaverse-LVIS, and ScanNet, as well as few-shot part segmentation on ShapeNetPart. SceneForge’s compositional augmentations are model-agnostic, consistently improving performance across multiple encoder architectures. Moreover, SceneForge improves 3D visual question answering on ScanQA, generalizes robustly to retrieval scenarios with increasing scene complexity, and showcases spatial reasoning capabilities by adapting spatial configurations to align precisely with textual instructions.

General machine learning (supervised, unsupervised, online, active, etc.)
Infrastructure (e.g., libraries, improved implementation and scalability, distributed solutions)
Machine learning for sciences (e.g. climate, health, life sciences, physics, social sciences)

Responses are confidential and will not be shared with reviewers, area chairs, or senior chairs. The PC Chairs will analyze aggregated data to understand how emerging technologies influence the research publication process. Please select all that apply below.
